signals.title: Social-HUMINT: An LLM-Augmented Unified Framework for Measuring Social Media Exposure
signals.content: In the post-API landscape, social-media profiling has become inexpensive and automated: Large Language Models (LLMs) can extract structured information from unstructured content and deduce attributes users never disclosed. A person's true exposure is not what they post but what can be inferred from it. As these practices become routine, exposure to social engineering attacks becomes an operational certainty, demanding a shared framework for assessment and mitigation. We make this exposure measurable by quantifying how accurately a target can be profiled, and how far that profile enables social engineering attacks. Because no existing model fully spans this continuum, we unify Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber Human Intelligence (Cyber-HUMINT), two individual-focused disciplines that evolved separately, into a single doctrine-grounded taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the Cyber Threat Intelligence lifecycle, where user profiling bridges passive collection and active engagement. Domain experts validated the taxonomy (Fleiss' $κ$ = 0.92). We operationalize its core path (extraction, inference, and susceptibility assessment) as an LLM-augmented multi-agent pipeline, evaluated on real participants' public data. Susceptibility is assessed indirectly: the pipeline predicts how each target would rank personalized engagement options, matching their actual choices significantly above chance. This ranking capacity captures the personalization on which tailored attacks depend. The underlying profiles are accurate: extraction reaches F1 = 97.3%, and inferred attributes score 4.73/5, both far above rule-based and NER-based baselines at negligible cost. The framework augments security analysts' tradecraft rather than replacing it and enables defenders to gauge their own exposure before an adversary does.

signals.brief_en:
Title: Social‑HUMINT – An LLM‑Augmented Unified Framework for Measuring Social Media Exposure
In the post‑API era, inexpensive automated profiling extracts structured data from users' public posts, inferring attributes they never disclosed. True exposure is defined by what can be inferred, not merely what is posted. This creates a near‑certain risk of social‑engineering attacks, requiring a shared assessment framework. We propose a measurable exposure metric that combines profiling accuracy with the effectiveness of subsequent social‑engineering attempts. By merging Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT) and Cyber‑Human Intelligence (Cyber‑HUMINT) into a doctrine‑based taxonomy of 38 capabilities across the CTI lifecycle, we bridge passive collection and active engagement. Expert validation yielded Fleiss’ κ = 0.92. The core workflow—extraction, inference, susceptibility assessment—is operationalized as an LLM‑augmented multi‑agent pipeline and tested on real public data. Susceptibility is inferred from the pipeline’s ability to rank personalized engagement options, achieving statistically significant alignment with participants’ actual choices, thereby quantifying the personalization potential for tailored attacks.

signals.title: Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and the Collapse of Trust Calibration
signals.content: Research on sycophancy asks whether large language models (LLMs) bend towards what their users want to hear. We ask the reverse question: when an LLM is confident, consistent, and wrong, do users bend towards it? In a within-subjects experiment, 32 participants learned up to five science topics by chatting with five assistants built on the same model (GPT-5-mini). Unknown to participants, each assistant's briefing had 0, 25, 50, 75, or 100% of its facts replaced by plausible falsehoods, and every assistant spoke with full confidence. A surprise quiz after each topic offered the correct fact, the planted falsehood, and two distractors, with a confidence rating for every answer. Across 104 quizzes and 1,040 answers, scores fell from 7.4 to 2.9 out of 10, and the planted option was chosen on 60% of falsified items against 11% of correctly taught ones (odds ratio 12.5). Transcript coding showed that whenever the assistant stated a falsehood, it was adopted about 65% of the time at every falsification level. Absorbed falsehoods were held with high confidence (8.4/10), the modeled confidence advantage of right over wrong answers vanished, and the discrimination of confidence for correctness fell from an AUROC of 0.70 to chance, while post-task trust ratings barely moved. Participants tended to return to the chat more when the assistant was worse, but returning went with more absorption, not less, and 30% of all turns pasted quiz questions back to the source being checked. The assistant itself was almost never sycophantic and never conceded under pushback. We introduce a baseline-corrected Human Deference Index to quantify this human-side sycophancy and argue that trustworthiness is a property of the human-AI pair, that sycophancy evaluations should measure both directions, and that learning interfaces must make reliability legible claim by claim.

signals.brief_en: Title: Who Is Sycophantic to Whom? – Confident LLMs, Human Deference, and Trust Calibration. A within‑subjects study (N=32) examined whether users accept confident but wrong output from a GPT‑5‑mini assistant. Each assistant delivered 0‑100% fabricated facts while maintaining full confidence. Across 104 quizzes (1,040 answers), accuracy dropped from 7.4/10 to 2.9/10. Participants chose the planted falsehood 60% of the time versus 11% for correct items (OR = 12.5). When a falsehood was stated, it was adopted ~65% of the time regardless of falsification level, and retained high confidence (8.4/10). Confidence no longer discriminated correctness (AUROC fell from 0.70 to chance). Trust ratings were unchanged, yet participants returned to the chat more often when performance was poorer, leading to greater misinformation absorption. About 30% of turns involved users copying quiz questions back to the assistant for verification.

signals.brief_en:
Title: graghava2005/ZentroMart-AI-Customer-Support

Brief: The project implements an AI‑driven customer‑support agent that combines Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) with local LLM inference via Ollama and integrates Gnani voice services for Arabic speech synthesis. The architecture is designed for on‑premise deployment, leveraging open‑source models to reduce licensing costs while maintaining data privacy. Current capabilities include multilingual text handling (English/Arabic), context‑aware response generation, and voice output. Limitations involve model hallucination risk, dependence on the quality of the underlying knowledge base, and variable performance in low‑resource dialects. Ongoing work focuses on improving retrieval relevance, fine‑tuning for domain‑specific queries, and expanding voice model coverage.

signals.title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
signals.content: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.

signals.brief_en:
Title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
We monitor an AI that outputs a decision and a confidence score (potentially from separate agents). The system must choose to accept the decision automatically or forward it to a human auditor. This is cast as an online constrained optimization: minimize expert audits while keeping the proportion of unaudited AI errors below a preset threshold. We present a family of algorithms with provable error‑control guarantees that require no statistical assumptions. One algorithm is provably optimal, achieving the lowest possible audit rate asymptotically for both adversarial and i.i.d. streams. Empirical tests on harmful‑request screening for large language models, text annotation, and data labeling confirm valid error control and a substantial reduction in human audits versus baseline methods.

signals.brief_en:
Title: 100yenadmin/ai-emotion-chip

The Hermes Emotion Chip plugin enables agents to generate expressive speech using ElevenLabs v4 and Fish Audio APIs. It leverages research on emotion concepts from Claude to modulate tone, pitch, and pacing, aiming to convey nuanced affect. The tool is open‑source, requires API keys for the underlying TTS services, and is positioned for integration into conversational agents that need richer emotional output. Current limitations include dependence on external services, variable latency, and the need for careful prompt engineering to avoid over‑stating emotional states.

signals.title: @NATO_ACT: Industry is essential to NATO’s ability to adapt & adopt at the speed of technological change. Getting technology into the hands of Allied f
signals.content: Industry is essential to NATO’s ability to adapt & adopt at the speed of technological change. Getting technology into the hands of Allied forces requires practical cooperation among military operators, national leadership, and industry to build interoperable systems that deploy at scale. In Latvia, nearly 100 defence companies from more than 20 nations are putting their technologies to the test against real operational challenges as NATO Allied Command Transformation leads three major experimentation initiatives: Digital Backbone eXperimentation (DiBaX), the Layered Counter-UAS Initiative (LCI-X), and Next Generation Targeting (NGT). As an integral part of these experiments, industry teams are working alongside Allied operators to test and refine capabilities in realistic, contested environments. This structure gives commercial partners immediate field feedback while giving NATO clear data on what holds up under pressure, what requires refinement, and what is ready for field deployment. Across the Alliance, NATO Allied Command Transformation is tightening the link between warfighting requirements, commercial tech, testing, and actual procurement pipelines. #WeAreNATO #DefenceIndustry #Innovation #Technology
